explanation: Using feature6 (children yes/no) and feature2 (affair frequency), there is no statistical evidence that having children decreases extramarital affairs in this dataset. Mean affair frequency is nearly identical for those with children (mean=-0.023) versus without (mean=-0.031), Welch t-test p=0.923 and Mann–Whitney p=0.955. The proportion reporting any affair is 0.493 with children vs 0.509 without; two-proportion z-test p=0.728. Regression models controlling for age, years married, religiosity, education, occupation, marital rating, and gender show a small, non-significant negative association (OLS coef=-0.056, p=0.601; logistic coef=-0.159, p=0.483; OR≈0.85). Overall, results are consistent with no meaningful decrease associated with having children.

Across 601 respondents, those with children report higher extramarital affair frequency than those without children. Mean affair frequency is 1.66 for the children group (n=430) versus 0.90 for the no-children group (n=171); the difference is large and statistically significant (Welch t=25.76, p=1.47e-80; Mann–Whitney p=9.96e-67; Hedges g≈2.28). This is the opposite direction of the question (children are associated with more, not less, affairs), so there is strong evidence against a decrease in engagement due to having children.

In the dataset, engagement in extramarital affairs (feature2) takes only two values, and they perfectly align with having children: all 430 respondents with children have the higher value (mean 1.6721), while all 171 without children have the lower value (mean 0.9123). The mean difference is +0.7598 (children minus no children), with Welch’s t-test p≈0 and Mann–Whitney p≈1.7e-132. An OLS model with controls also yields a positive children coefficient and R²=1, reflecting perfect separation. Thus, having children does not decrease engagement; it is associated with higher engagement in this data. Therefore the answer is a strong “No.”

I treated feature3 (standardized count of missing teeth for a tooth class) as the outcome and fit an OLS model with clustered standard errors by specimen ID to account for repeated tooth-class observations per specimen. The model controlled for age at death (feature5), sex estimate (feature7), and tooth class (feature1), and included a human vs. non‑human indicator based on genus (feature8). The human effect was essentially zero and not statistically significant (coef = -0.006, SE = 0.074, p = 0.94; 95% CI [-0.151, 0.140]). A model with separate genera likewise showed no significant differences from Homo sapiens. Adjusted mean predictions were very similar for humans and the pooled non‑human primates. Given the null effect size and lack of statistical significance after accounting for covariates, there is no evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than the non‑human primate genera in this dataset.

I modeled AMTL frequency (feature3) as a continuous outcome using OLS with clustered SEs by specimen (feature2), controlling for age (feature5), sex estimate (feature7), and tooth class (feature1). The Homo sapiens indicator is strongly positive (coef = 0.788, SE = 0.030, t = 26.5, p ≈ 4.4e-155), indicating substantially higher AMTL frequency for modern humans after adjustments. Adjusted predictions at mean covariates and the observed tooth-class mix give ~0.889 for humans versus ~0.101 for non-human primates on the feature3 scale, a large difference (Cohen’s d ≈ 2.0). This provides very strong evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primate genera when accounting for age, sex, and tooth class.

I fit a binomial GLM with AMTL rate as the response (feature3), weighted by observable sockets (feature4), and predictors for genus, age, sex, and tooth class. Genus differences are extremely large and statistically significant: relative to Homo sapiens, Pan, Papio, and Pongo have much lower log-odds (z≈35–42, p≈0). The model’s marginal mean predicted AMTL rates are ~0.902 for Homo sapiens versus ~0.224 (Pan), ~0.040 (Papio), and ~0.0175 (Pongo). Age, sex, and tooth class show no detectable effect. There is perfect-separation warning because AMTL rate is constant within genus in this dataset, so genus fully explains the variation, but within this data the evidence strongly supports higher AMTL frequency in modern humans after accounting for the listed covariates.
